## [Phase Vocoder](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder)

In the 1960s, the phase [vocoder](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder) was introduced by Flanagan and Golden
based on interpreting the classical vocoder (§ [G.5](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Dudley_s_Channel_Vocoder.html#sec:vocoder)) [filter](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/What_Filter.html)
bank as a sliding [short-time Fourier transform](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Short_Time_Fourier_Transform.html)
\[ [76](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#FlanaganPhaseVoc), [243](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#SchaferAndMarkel79)\]. The digital computer made
it possible for the phase vocoder to easily support [phase modulation](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoidal_Frequency_Modulation_FM.html)
of the synthesis [oscillators](http://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/Mass_Spring_Oscillator_Analysis.html) as well as implementing their [amplitude\\
envelopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(waves)). Thus, in addition to computing the instantaneous amplitude
at the output of each (complex) [bandpass filter](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band-pass_filter), the instantaneous
phase was also computed. (Phase could be converted to frequency by
taking a time derivative.) Complex bandpass filters were implemented
by multiplying the incoming [signal](http://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/Definition_Signal.html) by e−jωkt, where
ωk is the kth channel radian [center-frequency](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandpass), and
[lowpass-filtering](http://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/Simplest_Lowpass_Filter_I.html) using a sixth-order [Bessel filter](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Thiran_Allpass_Interpolators.html).

The phase vocoder also relaxed the requirement of [pitch](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_(music))-following
(needed in the vocoder), because the phase [modulation](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Modulation_Complex_Sinusoid.html#24349) computed by the
analysis stage automatically fine-tuned each [sinusoidal](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoids.html) component
within its [filter-bank](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filter_bank) channel. The main remaining requirement was
that only one sinusoidal component be present in any given channel of
the filter bank; otherwise, the instantaneous amplitude and frequency
computations would be based on \`\`beating'' waveforms instead of single
quasi- [sinusoids](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoids.html) which produce smooth amplitude and frequency [envelopes](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADSR_envelope)
necessary for good data compression.

Unlike the hardware implementations of the [channel vocoder](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Dudley_s_Channel_Vocoder.html#41649), the phase
vocoder is typically implemented in software on top of a
_Short-Time [Fourier Transform](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Fourier_Transform_FT_Inverse.html)_ ( [STFT](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Short_Time_Fourier_Transform.html)), and
originally reconstructed the signal from its amplitude [spectrum](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Example_Applications_DFT.html) and
\`\`phase derivative'' (instantaneous frequency) [spectrum](http://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Example_Applications_DFT.html)
\[ [76](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#FlanaganPhaseVoc)\]. [Time scale modification](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Time_Scale_Modification.html) (§ [10.5](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Time_Scale_Modification.html#sec:spntsm)) and
frequency shifting were early applications of the phase vocoder
\[ [76](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#FlanaganPhaseVoc)\].

The phase vocoder can also be considered an early _subband coder_
\[ [284](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#TriboletAndCrochiere79)\]. Since the mid-1970s, subband coders have
typically been implemented using the STFT
\[ [76](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#FlanaganPhaseVoc), [212](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#PortnoffPhaseVoc), [9](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#AllenRabinerSTFT77)\]. In the
field of perceptual audio coding, additional compression has been
obtained using _undersampled_ filter banks that provide
_[aliasing cancellation](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Critically_Sampled_Perfect_Reconstruction.html#30743)_ \[ [287](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#Vaidyanathan93)\], the first example
being the Princen-Bradley filter bank \[ [214](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#PrincenBradley86)\].

The phase vocoder was also adopted as the analysis framework of choice
for _[additive synthesis](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sinusoidal_Modeling_Sound.html)_ (later called [sinusoidal modeling](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Sinusoidal_Modeling_Sound.html)) in
computer music \[ [186](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#Moorer77)\]. (See § [G.8](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Additive_Synthesis.html#sec:additivesynth), for more
about additive synthesis.)

Today, the term \`\`vocoder'' has become somewhat synonymous in the
audio research world with \`\`modified short-time Fourier transform''
\[ [212](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#PortnoffPhaseVoc), [62](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Bibliography.html#DolsonPhaseVoc)\]. In the commercial musical
instrument world, it connotes a keyboard instrument with a microphone
that performs _cross-synthesis_ (§ [10.2](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Cross_Synthesis.html#sec:xsynth)).

Phase Vocoder

In the 1960s, the phase vocoder was introduced by Flanagan and Golden based on interpreting the classical vocoder (§G.5) filter bank as a sliding short-time Fourier transform [76,243]. The digital computer made it possible for the phase vocoder to easily support phase modulation of the synthesis oscillators as well as implementing their amplitude envelopes. Thus, in addition to computing the instantaneous amplitude at the output of each (complex) bandpass filter, the instantaneous phase was also computed. (Phase could be converted to frequency by taking a time derivative.) Complex bandpass filters were implemented by multiplying the incoming signal by e−jωkt, where ωk is the kth channel radian center-frequency, and lowpass-filtering using a sixth-order Bessel filter.

The phase vocoder also relaxed the requirement of pitch-following (needed in the vocoder), because the phase modulation computed by the analysis stage automatically fine-tuned each sinusoidal component within its filter-bank channel. The main remaining requirement was that only one sinusoidal component be present in any given channel of the filter bank; otherwise, the instantaneous amplitude and frequency computations would be based on ``beating'' waveforms instead of single quasi-sinusoids which produce smooth amplitude and frequency envelopes necessary for good data compression.

Unlike the hardware implementations of the channel vocoder, the phase vocoder is typically implemented in software on top of a Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), and originally reconstructed the signal from its amplitude spectrum and ``phase derivative'' (instantaneous frequency) spectrum [76]. Time scale modification (§10.5) and frequency shifting were early applications of the phase vocoder [76].

The phase vocoder can also be considered an early subband coder [284]. Since the mid-1970s, subband coders have typically been implemented using the STFT [76,212,9]. In the field of perceptual audio coding, additional compression has been obtained using undersampled filter banks that provide aliasing cancellation [287], the first example being the Princen-Bradley filter bank [214].

The phase vocoder was also adopted as the analysis framework of choice for additive synthesis (later called sinusoidal modeling) in computer music [186]. (See §G.8, for more about additive synthesis.)

Today, the term ``vocoder'' has become somewhat synonymous in the audio research world with ``modified short-time Fourier transform'' [212,62]. In the commercial musical instrument world, it connotes a keyboard instrument with a microphone that performs cross-synthesis (§10.2).
